name: Gleirschklamm
kurzbeschreibung: Gleirschklamm near Scharnitz in Naturpark Karwendel: pristine gorge trail along the roaring Gleirschbach with wooden walkways and timber floating history.
beschreibung:
Overview

The wildly romantic Gleirschklamm lies at the heart of the Naturpark Karwendel – Austria's largest nature park – in the municipality of Scharnitz in the Seefeld region at around 1,000 metres above sea level. Wedged between the rugged rocky peaks of the Erlspitzgruppe and the Gleirsch-Halltal-Kette, the gorge ranks among the most pristine and unspoiled natural wonders of North Tyrol. Along the thundering Gleirschbach, a spectacular, narrow rocky trail leads through a dramatic canyon landscape characterized by cascading rapids, deep blue plunge pools, and towering limestone walls.

Geology & Karwendel Timber Floating

The geological origins of the Gleirschklamm date back over 230 million years to the Mesozoic era (Triassic period): the sheer gorge walls consist of massive Wettersteinkalk (Wetterstein limestone), which was originally formed in a shallow tropical sea. Uplifted by tectonic forces and sliced through by the relentless deep erosion of the meltwater torrent, the mountain stream unearths fossil remains of prehistoric marine organisms to this day. In addition to its geology, the gorge is intimately tied to Tyrolean economic history: for centuries, the Gleirschtal valley was a vital hub of the Karwendel-Holztrift (timber floating). Massive quantities of felled roundwood were driven through the narrow rocky chasm during the spring snowmelt and onwards via the Isar river to supply the immense boiling pans of the Saline Hall in Tirol with vital firewood. To clear dreaded log jams in the tight rocky bends, lumberjacks chiseled the so-called Schachener Triftsteig directly into the rock walls. Today, this arduous era is commemorated in the lovingly curated Museum Holzerhütte at the valley entrance in Scharnitz. The modern gorge trail, about one kilometre long, has been gently modernized and leads over solid wooden footbridges, secured bridges, and airy rock shelves directly above the churning whitewater.

Visit & Arrival

The Gleirschklamm is freely accessible during snow-free months from mid-May to late October (during the winter months from November to May, the gorge is officially closed by authorities due to avalanche and rockfall hazards). Access to the canyon is completely free of charge (€0.00 admission). Arrival by public transport: Take the S-Bahn Tirol (line S6) or the Karwendelbahn REX directly to Bahnhof Scharnitz; from there, it is about a 45-minute walk past the Naturpark-Infozentrum and Scharnitzer Alm to the gorge entrance. By car: Via the B177 Seefelder Straße (from the Inntal valley over the Zirler Berg or from Bavaria via Mittenwald) directly to Scharnitz; large paid hiker car parks are available in the district of „In der Länd“ (Karwendel car parks P1 to P5 on Hinterautalstraße).

Tips

Due to the narrow rocky path, wet wooden planks, and uneven steps, the Gleirschklamm is absolutely not barrier-free and is unsuitable for strollers; sure-footed mountain boots with sturdy treaded soles and a head for heights are essential. The trail is not recommended for small toddlers. Highly rewarding is the Gleirschklamm-Rundwanderung (circular hike, walking time approx. 3.5 hours): after traversing the gorge, follow the forest road further to the idyllic Möslalm (1,262 m) for a traditional Tyrolean cold-cut platter (Brettljause), returning via the panoramic Nederweg trail through shady mountain forest back to Scharnitz.
preis: Kostenlos frei zugänglich (Parkplatz In der Länd gebührenpflichtig)
oeffnungszeiten: Mitte Mai bis Ende Oktober tagsüber geöffnet (im Winter gesperrt)
